title: Delhi High Court Upholds Telegram Ban, Expands Government's Power to Block Entire Platforms
excerpt: The ruling establishes that India's Section 69A extends to blocking full applications — not just specific content — setting a precedent that digital rights groups warn could affect every platform operating in the country.
body:
• The Delhi High Court ruled that India's Section 69A of the IT Act empowers the government to block entire platforms — not just specific content — in a landmark decision dismissing Telegram's challenge.
  • The temporary ban was imposed ahead of the NEET-UG 2026 re-exam after Telegram was used to circulate leaked examination papers and fraudulent content.
  • Digital rights organisations warn the precedent treats "the speech of a whole population as a single switch to be turned off."
  • Telegram has more than 150 million users in India, making it one of the country's most widely used messaging platforms.

The Ruling

Justice Tejas Karia of the Delhi High Court delivered a 39-page verdict that significantly expanded the understood scope of the Indian government's power to restrict online platforms. The court held that "information" under Section 2(1)(v) of the IT Act includes codes, computer programmes and software — and therefore encompasses entire applications, not merely individual pieces of content hosted on them.

https://x.com/orfonline/status/2079126169195290792

"The blocking power under Section 69A of the IT Act extends beyond individual pieces of content," the bench ruled, establishing that years of URL-by-URL blocking practice had simply been the government choosing not to use its full statutory authority.

"The court's statutory interpretation — that any application qualifies as a "computer resource" containing "information" under the Act — applies generically to any software platform."

Why Telegram Was Blocked

The case arose after the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an emergency order blocking Telegram in India until June 22, 2026, ahead of the NEET-UG re-examination. The National Testing Agency and the Ministry of Education had flagged Telegram as a hub for the circulation of leaked question papers, with the platform's message-editing feature being used by fraudsters to create fake evidence of leaks by replacing attached files while retaining original timestamps.

Telegram argued it had proactively taken down unlawful NEET-related content, including deploying AI and machine learning tools. It contended that blocking an entire platform used by 150 million Indians was disproportionate when the government's concerns related to a subset of users.

What Rights Groups Are Saying

The Internet Freedom Foundation questioned the court's interpretation, arguing that the Supreme Court's earlier Shreya Singhal decision had upheld Section 69A precisely because its power was understood to be narrowly drawn and directed at specific information.

"It is the difference between removing a few pages from a library and padlocking the entire building," the IFF said in a statement, warning that the precedent "carries consequences for the open internet that extend well beyond this case."

"Blocking of a platform is different from blocking of a group, is different from blocking of an account, is different from blocking of a post — the restriction affects lawful users, businesses, and speech across the platform."

— Nikhil Pahwa, Founder, MediaNama

The Broader Implications

Legal analysts note the reasoning is not specific to Telegram's technical architecture. The court's statutory interpretation — that any application qualifies as a "computer resource" containing "information" under the Act — applies generically to any software platform. That includes WhatsApp, Signal, X and every other communication tool operating in India.

The court did apply a proportionality test, holding that the temporary nature of the block — limited to the examination period — satisfied the constitutional threshold. But critics argue the precedent separates the power from the specific facts, meaning future governments could invoke it for broader or longer-lasting restrictions.

What's Next

The temporary ban has expired, and Telegram is once again accessible in India. But the legal precedent stands. The government also directed Telegram to disable its message-editing feature in India until June 30, a narrower restriction that raises its own questions about platform sovereignty and feature-level regulatory control. For India's 150 million Telegram users — and the broader digital ecosystem — the ruling marks a significant shift in the balance of power between platforms and the state.
nri_angle: The ruling has implications for digital communications across India and raises concerns among the diaspora about the government's expanding authority over messaging platforms they rely on to stay connected with family.
